Not yet — subtraction is not associative, so the grouping changes the answer.

exercises.solution: It prints `9 3`. The right fold is `10 - (4 - 3) = 10 - 1 = 9`; the left fold is `(10 - 4) - 3 = 3`. For associative operators like `+` the direction does not change the result, but for `-` it does.

feedback.message: Not yet — the template can be instantiated with `T = char` or `T = float`, which are exact matches. An exact match beats a promotion.

hints: For each call, list the candidates: the template (with `T` deduced from the argument) and the plain function.
An exact match beats a promotion; on a tie, a non-template beats a template. Specialisations are only consulted after the primary template is chosen.
exercises.solution: It prints `int plain-double generic generic`. `show(1)`: the template with `T = int` is an exact match, the plain function needs a conversion; the template wins, and *then* its `int` specialisation is used. `show(1.0)`: the template (`T = double`) and the plain function are both exact; on a tie the non-template wins. `show('c')`: the template with `T = char` is exact, while `char` to `double` is a conversion, so the generic version runs. `show(2.0f)`: `T = float` is exact, while the plain function would need a promotion to `double`, so again the generic version runs.

feedback.message: Not yet — a `const char*` is a pointer. Does a pointer have a member function `size()`?

hints: A concept is true when every requirement inside the requires-expression would compile.
exercises.solution: It prints `true false false`. `std::string` has a `size()` member returning `std::size_t`. `int` has no members at all. `const char*` is a pointer, which has no member functions either, even though it often points at text; you would measure it with `std::strlen` or by converting it to a `std::string_view`.

exercises.prompt: Given `template <typename A, typename B> struct Pair { A first; B second; };`, what type does `Pair p{"Nairobi", 1899};` give `p`?

options.label: `Pair<const char*, int>`
options.feedback: Yes. The string literal decays to `const char*` and `1899` is an `int`.

options.label: `Pair<std::string, int>`
options.feedback: Not yet — deduction uses the argument's own type. A string literal is an array of `const char`, which decays to `const char*`; nothing turns it into a `std::string`.

options.label: It does not compile: the template arguments must be written out.
options.feedback: Not yet — class template argument deduction (C++17) fills them in. For an aggregate like this one, with no constructor or deduction guide, it needs C++20, which this course uses.

options.label: `Pair<auto, auto>`
options.feedback: Not yet — template arguments are always concrete types after deduction.

hints: What is the type of a string literal once it decays?
exercises.solution: `Pair<const char*, int>`. Class template argument deduction looks at the initialisers' types exactly as function template deduction would. If you want a `std::string`, write `Pair p{std::string{"Nairobi"}, 1899};` or use the `s` literal suffix: `"Nairobi"s`.

exercises.prompt: A team declares `template <typename T> T clamp_to_range(T x, T lo, T hi);` in `util.hpp` and defines it in `util.cpp`. Code in `main.cpp` calls `clamp_to_range(5, 0, 3)`. What happens?

options.label: It compiles, but linking fails with an undefined reference, because `util.cpp` never instantiated the template for `int`.
options.feedback: Yes. `main.cpp` saw only the declaration, so it expects the `int` version to exist elsewhere; `util.cpp` had no reason to generate it.

options.label: It works, like any other function split between a header and a source file.
options.feedback: Not yet — a template is not a function until it is instantiated, and instantiation needs the body.

options.label: The compiler reports an error in `main.cpp` saying the template has no body.
options.feedback: Not yet — the compiler accepts a call to a declared template and assumes an instantiation exists somewhere. The problem shows up later.

options.label: The template is instantiated at run time, the first time it is called.
options.feedback: Not yet — C++ templates are always instantiated by the compiler, never at run time.

hints: To generate `clamp_to_range<int>`, what does the compiler need to see?
Which step of the build reports a missing function?
exercises.solution: The call compiles in `main.cpp` against the declaration, and the compiler emits a reference to `clamp_to_range<int>`. But `util.cpp` contains only the template, and since nothing in that file uses it with `int`, no `int` version is generated. The **linker** then reports an undefined reference. The usual fix is to define the template in the header. (Explicitly instantiating `template int clamp_to_range<int>(int, int, int);` in `util.cpp` also works when the set of types is fixed.)

exercises.prompt: In which of these situations are **virtual functions** (run-time polymorphism) a better fit than templates? Select all that apply.

options.label: A drawing program keeps one list of shapes of many kinds, chosen by the user while it runs.
options.feedback: Yes. One container holding objects of different types is the classic case for a base class and pointers.

options.label: A numerical library offers a fast `dot_product` for `float`, `double` and complex numbers.
options.feedback: Not yet — the types are known when the code is compiled, and inlining the arithmetic matters. That is template territory.

options.label: An application loads audio-effect plug-ins, compiled by other people, from shared libraries at start-up.
options.feedback: Yes. The application was compiled before the plug-ins existed, so it can only talk to them through a fixed run-time interface.

options.label: A sorting function should work for any container of comparable elements.
options.feedback: Not yet — this is what `std::ranges::sort`, a constrained template, does.

hints: Ask of each case: are all the types known where the code is compiled? Must different types live in one container?
exercises.solution: Virtual functions fit (a) and (c): objects of different types in one collection, and types that did not exist when the code using them was compiled. Templates fit (b) and (d): the types are known at compile time and performance benefits from code specialised for each one.
